title: Nonlinearity
intro: No amplifier is perfectly linear. For the mild nonlinearity of a well-designed precision circuit, a short power series describes everything: harmonics, the deviation from a straight line, and how differential operation and feedback reduce them (Razavi, Section 14.1).

blocks.text: Polynomial model and the straight-line metric

$\alpha_1$ is the small-signal gain around $x = 0$. A practical single number: over the input range, draw the straight line through the end points of the real characteristic, find the largest deviation $\Delta V$, and divide by the full output swing. For an odd characteristic $y = \alpha_1 x + \alpha_3 x^3$ over $\pm x_{max}$ the largest deviation is at $x = x_{max}/\sqrt{3}$, and

blocks.caption: Relative nonlinearity grows with the square of the swing.

blocks.text: Harmonics and THD
With $x = A\cos\omega t$, the square term gives a DC shift and a second harmonic, the cube term a third harmonic plus a change in the fundamental:

blocks.tex: y = \alpha_1 A\cos\omega t + \frac{\alpha_2A^2}{2}\left[1 + \cos 2\omega t\right] + \frac{\alpha_3A^3}{4}\left[3\cos\omega t + \cos 3\omega t\right] + \cdots

blocks.text: The $n$th harmonic grows roughly as $A^n$. Total harmonic distortion sums the power of all harmonics relative to the fundamental; for a third-order model

Individual ratios: $\mathrm{HD}_2 = \alpha_2A/(2\alpha_1)$ and $\mathrm{HD}_3 = \alpha_3A^2/(4\alpha_1)$ in amplitude. As a scale, high-quality audio wants about $-80$ dB (0.01%) and video about $-60$ dB (0.1%).
Differential circuits

A differential circuit driven differentially is odd-symmetric, $f(-x) = -f(x)$, so every even coefficient vanishes and no even harmonics appear. The gain in linearity is large even beyond that. Compare a CS stage and a differential pair with the same gain $g_mR_D$ and the same overdrive. The square law gives, for the CS drain current,
while expanding the pair's $I_{D1} - I_{D2}$ for small inputs leaves only a cubic term:
At $V_m = 0.2(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$ that is 5% against 0.125%. The pair uses twice the current, but doubling the CS stage's current at fixed $W/L$ only cuts its distortion by $\sqrt{2}$.
Negative feedback

Nonlinearity is gain that varies with signal level, and feedback desensitises the gain, so it suppresses distortion too. For a core amplifier $\alpha_1 x + \alpha_2 x^2$ in a loop with feedback factor $\beta$, assume the output is $a\cos\omega t + b\cos 2\omega t$, push it round the loop and keep first-order terms in the small quantities:

blocks.caption: Relative second harmonic falls by $(1 + \beta\alpha_1)^2$ for the same input, while the gain falls by $1 + \beta\alpha_1$.

blocks.text: A useful design shortcut: if the small-signal gain falls monotonically toward the ends of the range (the usual case), the end-point nonlinearity of a feedback amplifier is always smaller than its gain error $\approx 1/(\beta A_0)$. So choosing the open-loop gain to meet a gain-error spec also guarantees the linearity spec. It is pessimistic, and costly when short-channel devices make gain scarce.
Capacitor nonlinearity

Real capacitors vary with voltage, $C = C_0(1 + \alpha_1V + \alpha_2V^2 + \cdots)$, so charge is $Q = \int_0^V C\,dV$, not $CV$. In the SC non-inverting amplifier with nominal gain $M$ ($C_1 = MC_2$) and a linear coefficient $\alpha_1$ in both capacitors, equating the charge given up by $C_1$ with the charge taken by $C_2$ gives
The error vanishes for $M = 1$ (the two capacitors see the same voltage history) and grows with the gain.
Sampling-switch nonlinearity

A switch's on-resistance changes with the signal, so the tiny phase lag $R_{on}C\omega_0$ of a sampler changes over the cycle. With a periodic input, $R_{on}(t) = R_0 + R_1\cos\omega_0t + R_2\cos 2\omega_0t + \cdots$, and for small phase excursions the output picks up a second harmonic of amplitude $V_0R_1C\omega_0/2$ and a third of $V_0R_2C\omega_0/2$:

A complementary switch has an $R_{on}$ that peaks mid-range (mobility degradation), so it varies at twice the input frequency: $R_1 \approx 0$ and the third harmonic dominates. A differential sampler removes the even harmonics.

blocks.title: Harmonic distortion
blocks.text: $\alpha_1 = 10$, $\alpha_2 = 1\text{ V}^{-1}$, $\alpha_3 = -2\text{ V}^{-2}$ and $A = 0.1$ V. Find $\mathrm{HD}_2$, $\mathrm{HD}_3$ and the THD.
solution: THD $= (0.005^2 + 0.0005^2)/(1 - 0.0015)^2 = 2.53\times 10^{-5}$, i.e. $-46$ dB: the second harmonic dominates.

blocks.title: End-point nonlinearity
blocks.text: A differential amplifier has $\alpha_1 = 10$ and $\alpha_3 = -2\text{ V}^{-2}$ and is driven over $\pm 0.2$ V. Find its end-point nonlinearity.

blocks.title: Feedback and the second harmonic
blocks.text: A core amplifier with $\alpha_1 = 50$ and $\alpha_2 = 5\text{ V}^{-1}$ is driven with $V_m = 10$ mV. Find the relative second harmonic open loop, and with $\beta = 0.18$.
solution: $\beta\alpha_1 = 9$, so it falls by $(1 + 9)^2 = 100$ to $5\times 10^{-6}$ (the gain falls from 50 to 5).
